query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating, promoting surface segregation of oxidation‐prone elements (such as Cr and Fe) via a brief post-deposition anneal will lead to the rapid formation of a continuous, nanocrystalline oxide film at the grain boundaries during high‐temperature sliding, which in turn reduces adhesive wear and suppresses severe plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally deposited FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy thin coating on a metal substrate with a roughly homogeneous distribution of elements and a moderately sized, as-deposited microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment (in a moderately reducing atmosphere to limit premature oxidation) designed to induce elemental segregation—especially of Cr and Fe—to the grain boundaries, followed by exposure to sliding wear in an oxidative environment at high temperature.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted at high temperatures (approximately 600–800°C) in ambient air, under moderate sliding load and speed conditions that generate frictional heating without immediate catastrophic failure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a fine, continuous, and nanocrystalline oxide film (e.g., Cr- and Fe-based oxides) along the grain boundaries and wear surface, originating from the selectively segregated elements.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment enriches grain boundaries with oxidation‐prone species, and upon sliding at elevated temperatures, these species oxidize rapidly to form a protective oxide film. This film acts as a barrier that lowers adhesive interactions, minimizes direct metal contact, and distributes the sliding load more uniformly, thereby reducing both wear rate and the extent of local plastic (microscopic) deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline coating, the annealed coatings with enhanced grain-boundary segregation will exhibit a lower wear rate and reduced microscopic deformation (e.g., less severe plastic flow and micro-cracking) under the specified high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional metal substrate that lacks the pre-engineered microstructural segregation and hence forms a less protective surface oxide during sliding at high temperature.
generation.boundary: These improvements are expected to hold in the tested regime (600–800°C sliding in ambient air at moderate load/speed). Results may differ under extreme sliding conditions or in environments with significantly different oxygen partial pressures.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the degree of segregation achievable without detrimental effects, and the uniformity and stability of the resultant oxide film during prolonged sliding. Furthermore, the interplay between the coating and substrate might introduce additional variables not fully captured within this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on an identical conventional metal substrate: one set receives the controlled post-deposition annealing treatment to induce grain-boundary segregation, while the other set remains in the as-deposited state. Conduct sliding wear tests at around 700°C in ambient air. Characterize the wear track through quantitative wear volume/depth analysis, friction coefficient measurements, and detailed microstructural/chemical analysis (using SEM, TEM, and EDS) before and after sliding.
measurements: Continuity and thickness of the surface oxide film (via SEM/TEM)
Evidence of grain boundary segregation and its correlation with oxide formation (via EDS mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction (relative to the baseline) in wear rate and microscopic deformation, or if the expected continuous oxide film does not form (as confirmed by microstructural analysis), then the hypothesis—that promoting grain-boundary segregation to induce protective oxide film formation governs improved wear resistance—would be falsified.
